ppvProviders.name: HBO
ppvProviders.focus: World-title fights and superfights on premium cable
ppvProviders.blurb: Home Box Office, the premium cable network whose boxing franchise made it the destination for the sport's biggest stars.
ppvProviders.ethos: HBO treats boxing as prestige programming. It wants champions, unbeaten stars and fights that feel like events, and it pays more than anyone to get them. A routine defence will not interest it; a pound-for-pound name will.
ppvProviders.history: HBO broadcast its first fight in 1973, George Foreman's demolition of Joe Frazier in Kingston, and built its reputation on Ali, Leonard, Hagler and Holmes. By the mid-1980s its boxing series was the most important television outlet in the sport.

ppvProviders.name: Showtime
ppvProviders.blurb: Premium cable channel and the main rival to HBO for championship boxing.
ppvProviders.ethos: Showtime competes with HBO by being willing to take fights its rival will not, building rivalries and moving quickly into pay-per-view. It values title fights but will gamble on an exciting matchup.
ppvProviders.history: Launched in 1976, Showtime moved seriously into boxing in the mid-1980s. Its championship series and pay-per-view arm became the long-term home of Don King's stable and later of Mike Tyson's comeback.

ppvProviders.name: ABC Sports
ppvProviders.focus: Free-to-air title fights and Olympians on Wide World of Sports
ppvProviders.blurb: The American network that brought world-title boxing to free television on Saturday afternoons.
ppvProviders.ethos: ABC uses boxing to win weekend ratings. It likes recognisable names, American champions and Olympic heroes, and with the 1984 gold medallists turning pro it wants to follow their careers from their debuts.
ppvProviders.history: ABC's Wide World of Sports and Howard Cosell made boxing a fixture of American network television in the 1960s and 1970s. It carried Ali's fights and the US Championship tournament, and remained a major buyer of title fights into the 1980s.

ppvProviders.name: CBS Sports
ppvProviders.blurb: CBS Sports, a weekend network buyer of American title fights and contenders.
ppvProviders.ethos: CBS buys fights for its weekend sports anthology shows. It prefers American fighters and clear title stakes, and after the Duk Koo Kim tragedy in 1982 its executives pay close attention to fighter safety.
ppvProviders.history: CBS carried major title fights through the late 1970s and 1980s, including Ray Mancini's 1982 bout with Duk Koo Kim, whose death led to shorter title fights.

ppvProviders.name: ESPN
ppvProviders.focus: Weekly cable cards for prospects and contenders
ppvProviders.blurb: The all-sports cable network whose weekly boxing series is where prospects are built.
ppvProviders.ethos: ESPN needs fights every week, not once a year. It pays modest fees, values action and a steady stream of unbeaten prospects and contenders, and gives promoters a weekly showcase for their young fighters.
ppvProviders.history: ESPN began carrying boxing almost from its 1979 launch, and its weekly Top Rank Boxing series became the main development path for American prospects in the 1980s.

ppvProviders.name: USA Network
ppvProviders.focus: Tuesday Night Fights: action bouts between contenders
ppvProviders.blurb: Basic cable channel known for its weekly Tuesday Night Fights.
ppvProviders.ethos: USA Network wants entertaining fights at a low price. Its audience likes punchers and upsets, so it is a good platform for fringe contenders who need a breakthrough win.
ppvProviders.history: USA Network's weekly fight series, later branded Tuesday Night Fights, began in the early 1980s and ran for nearly two decades, giving hundreds of contenders national exposure.

ppvProviders.name: ITV
ppvProviders.focus: British title nights and homegrown stars
ppvProviders.blurb: Britain's commercial network, which built its schedule around domestic stars and rivalries.
ppvProviders.ethos: ITV wants British fighters in big domestic fights, especially rivalries that can fill a football ground. It pays well for a homegrown favourite and pays little for anyone else.
ppvProviders.history: ITV carried British boxing from its earliest years and by the late 1980s was the main home of the domestic scene, including the Benn, Eubank and Watson rivalry.

ppvProviders.name: BBC Sport
ppvProviders.focus: Highlights and live British title fights
ppvProviders.blurb: The BBC's sports department, home of Harry Carpenter's commentary for most of British boxing's modern history.
ppvProviders.ethos: The BBC treats boxing as a national sporting tradition. It values British champions and clean, competitive fights, and it avoids anything that looks like a mismatch or a circus.
ppvProviders.history: BBC television covered boxing from the late 1930s, and Harry Carpenter's commentary accompanied most of the great British nights until the corporation stepped back from the sport in the mid-1990s.

ppvProviders.name: Televisa
ppvProviders.focus: Mexican idols and world-title nights from Mexico
ppvProviders.blurb: Mexico's dominant broadcaster, whose Saturday fight broadcasts made national idols of Mexican champions.
ppvProviders.ethos: Televisa wants Mexican champions in exciting fights, ideally in Mexico and ideally against a rival from Puerto Rico or the United States. It is closely tied to the WBC.
ppvProviders.history: Since its formation in 1973 Televisa has broadcast the careers of Mexico's champions, from Salvador Sánchez to Julio César Chávez, and its Saturday fight shows draw some of the largest boxing audiences in the world.

ppvProviders.name: Nippon TV
ppvProviders.focus: Japanese world-title fights in the lighter divisions
ppvProviders.blurb: Japanese terrestrial network that televises world-title fights involving Japanese fighters.
ppvProviders.ethos: Japanese television pays well for world-title fights featuring Japanese challengers and champions in the lighter divisions. It wants clean, well-produced events in Tokyo.
ppvProviders.history: Japanese networks have televised world-title boxing since the 1950s, when Yoshio Shirai was flyweight champion, and their broadcast money is why so many lighter-weight title fights are staged in Japan.

organisations.label: WBC
organisations.ethos: The WBC sees itself as the senior body in professional boxing. Under president José Sulaimán it has pushed safety reforms such as 12-round title fights and pre-fight medical checks, and it enforces mandatory challengers. Critics say it is too close to Don King and too quick to rank his fighters.
organisations.history: The WBC was founded in Mexico City in 1963 by commissions from eleven countries, to give boxing an international governing body outside the American NBA. José Sulaimán became president in 1975, and in 1983 the WBC cut title fights from 15 rounds to 12 after Duk Koo Kim's death.

organisations.label: WBA
organisations.ethos: The WBA is the oldest sanctioning body and claims the longest championship lineage. Its world ratings are dominated by Latin American officials, and Venezuela and Panama have great influence. It keeps 15-round title fights and often recognises different champions from the WBC.
organisations.history: It was founded in 1921 as the National Boxing Association, a group of American state commissions, and renamed the World Boxing Association in 1962. By the 1980s Latin American members controlled it, and Gilberto Mendoza became president in 1982.

organisations.label: IBF
organisations.ethos: The IBF presents itself as an American alternative to the Latin-dominated WBA and the Mexico-based WBC. It keeps a strict mandatory-challenger system and quickly recognised established champions such as Larry Holmes and Marvin Hagler, which gave it credibility.
organisations.history: Robert W. Lee and members of the United States Boxing Association broke away from the WBA in 1983 after losing the WBA presidential election, and formed the USBA-International, renamed the IBF in 1984. Its early recognition of Holmes and Hagler made it a major world body within a year.

organisations.label: WBO
organisations.ethos: The WBO is the newest of the four major bodies. It looks for champions and title fights the other bodies have left behind, and promoters in Europe and Puerto Rico rely on it.
organisations.history: A group of Puerto Rican and Dominican businessmen broke away from the WBA at its 1988 convention and founded the WBO in San Juan. For its first decade it was seen as a minor title, before champions such as Chris Eubank, Naseem Hamed and Oscar De La Hoya made it widely accepted.

organisations.label: EBU
organisations.ethos: The EBU runs European championships and treats them as a real step towards a world title. It enforces its mandatory challengers, and its champions are usually ranked by the world bodies.
organisations.history: The EBU was formed in 1946 as the successor to the International Boxing Union (founded 1920) and has its headquarters in Rome. Its European title is one of the oldest continental championships in the sport.

organisations.label: NABF
organisations.ethos: The NABF is the WBC's regional body for North America. Its title is used to move American, Mexican and Canadian contenders into the world ratings.
organisations.history: The NABF was founded in 1969 and is affiliated with the WBC. Its belts have been held by many future world champions, including Muhammad Ali and Larry Holmes.

organisations.label: OPBF
organisations.ethos: The OPBF serves boxing in Asia and the Pacific, especially Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Thailand and Australia. Its titles prepare fighters in the lighter weights for world-title challenges.
organisations.history: The Oriental Boxing Federation was founded in 1954 and later became the Oriental and Pacific Boxing Federation. Japanese commissions have dominated it, and it works with the WBC.

organisations.label: ABU
organisations.ethos: The ABU runs continental championships across Africa. Its title is the usual route to a world ranking for Ghanaian, Nigerian, Zambian and other African fighters.
organisations.history: The African Boxing Union was founded in 1973 to organise continental titles. It works with the WBC, and its strongest members are Ghana and Nigeria.

organisations.label: AIBA
organisations.ethos: AIBA governs Olympic-style amateur boxing. It runs the World Championships and the Olympic tournament and treats headguards and computer scoring as essential to fighter safety.
organisations.history: AIBA was founded in London in 1946 to replace the earlier international amateur federation. Its Olympic and World Championship tournaments produce most of the future professional stars.

organisations.label: USBA
organisations.ethos: The USBA awards the US national championship. Because there is no federal boxing commission, it coordinates ratings across the state commissions.
organisations.history: The USBA was formed in the 1970s to award a national championship. In 1983 its leaders founded the IBF, and the two organisations have stayed closely linked.

organisations.label: BBBofC
organisations.ethos: The BBBofC licenses every professional in Britain and awards the British title and the Lonsdale Belt. It is cautious and strict on medical safety.
organisations.history: The Board was founded in 1929 to take over from the National Sporting Club as the sport's regulator in Britain. Its Lonsdale Belt, first awarded in 1909, is one of the most prized domestic titles in boxing.

organisations.label: CBPPR
organisations.fullName: Comisión de Boxeo Profesional de Puerto Rico
organisations.ethos: The commission regulates professional boxing on the island and awards Puerto Rican titles. Puerto Rico produces world champions out of proportion to its size.
organisations.history: Puerto Rico has had a professional boxing commission for most of the twentieth century. It has overseen the careers of world champions from Sixto Escobar to Wilfredo Gómez.

organisations.label: FCB
organisations.ethos: Cuba banned professional boxing in 1962, so the federation runs only amateur boxing. Its national team is the strongest amateur programme in the world.
organisations.history: After professional boxing was banned in 1962, Cuba built a state amateur system that has produced Olympic champions such as Teófilo Stevenson. Cuban fighters can turn professional only by defecting.

organisations.label: FAB
organisations.ethos: The FAB regulates professional boxing in Argentina and awards national titles. Luna Park is the centre of its fight calendar.
organisations.history: Founded in 1920, the FAB has overseen Argentine boxing from Luis Ángel Firpo to Carlos Monzón and has worked closely with Luna Park promoter Tito Lectoure.

organisations.label: FEB
organisations.ethos: The FEB regulates both amateur and professional boxing in Spain and awards Spanish national titles.
organisations.history: Spanish boxing had its best years in the 1960s and 1970s with champions such as José Legrá and Pedro Carrasco. The federation's title remains the main step towards European honours.

organisations.label: GAB
organisations.ethos: The GAB is the government agency that licenses professional boxers in the Philippines and sanctions national titles. It also oversees other professional sports and gaming.
organisations.history: The GAB was created in 1951. It regulated boxing in the years of Flash Elorde and of the 1975 Thrilla in Manila.

organisations.label: BUI
organisations.ethos: The BUI regulates professional boxing in the Republic of Ireland and awards Irish titles. The country's amateur system is strong, but its professional scene is small.
organisations.history: The BUI took on the regulation of Irish professional boxing as the sport recovered from decades in which Irish professionals had to box mainly in Britain.

organisations.label: KBC
organisations.ethos: The KBC licenses professional boxers in South Korea and awards national titles. In the 1980s Korea is one of the busiest countries in the world for title fights in the lighter weights.
organisations.history: Korean professional boxing grew quickly after Kim Ki-soo won a world title in 1966. By the mid-1980s Korean champions such as Chang Jung-koo held world titles in several of the lighter divisions.

organisations.label: FECOMBOX
organisations.fullName: Federación Mexicana de Comisiones de Box Profesional
organisations.ethos: FECOMBOX coordinates Mexico's state boxing commissions and awards Mexican national titles. It works closely with the WBC, which also has its headquarters in Mexico City.
organisations.history: Mexican boxing has long been regulated by city and state commissions, led by the Comisión de Box del Distrito Federal. The federation was formed to coordinate these commissions and their national champions.

organisations.label: NZPBA
organisations.ethos: The NZPBA sanctions professional boxing in New Zealand and awards national titles. New Zealand's professional scene is small.
organisations.history: New Zealand's professional scene was strongest in the early twentieth century with Bob Fitzsimmons and Tom Heeney, and has survived on small domestic shows since.

organisations.label: NBBofC
organisations.ethos: The NBBofC licenses Nigerian professionals and awards national titles. Most top Nigerian fighters move to Britain or the United States to advance their careers.
organisations.history: Nigeria produced world champions Hogan 'Kid' Bassey and Dick Tiger in the 1950s and 1960s. The Board has tried to keep a domestic scene going in Lagos since independence.

organisations.label: JBC
organisations.ethos: The JBC is one of the strictest commissions in the world. It requires every boxer to belong to a licensed gym, enforces medical standards and controls which world bodies Japanese fighters may box for.
organisations.history: The JBC was founded in 1952, the year Yoshio Shirai became Japan's first world champion. Its gym-licensing system has made Japan a leading country in the lighter weight divisions.

organisations.label: FPBR
organisations.ethos: The FPBR regulates the young professional sport in Russia. It is trying to turn the country's large amateur system into professional champions.
organisations.history: Professional boxing was banned in the Soviet Union. It was legalised only as the Soviet Union broke up, and the Russian federation was formed in the early 1990s to license a new generation of professionals.

agencies.name: Voluntary Anti-Doping Organisation
agencies.blurb: No-notice, year-round, and the one the clean fighters ask for by name.

agencies.name: United States Anti-Doping Organisation
agencies.blurb: The full olympic-standard programme. Thorough, expensive, slow to clear a name.

agencies.name: European Anti-Doping
agencies.blurb: Runs the continental programme and shares its findings with the bodies.

agencies.name: Clean Boxing Organisation
agencies.blurb: Sanctioning-body testing. Broad enrolment, lighter touch, and it shows.

agencies.name: Commission screening
agencies.blurb: The statutory minimum on fight week. Catches the careless and little else.

magazines.name: The Ring
magazines.tagline: The Bible of Boxing, publishing ratings and world champions since 1922.

magazines.name: KO Magazine
magazines.tagline: Knockouts, rankings and the fights everyone wants to see.

magazines.name: Boxing Illustrated
magazines.tagline: American boxing's monthly of stars, contenders and comebacks.

magazines.name: Boxing News
magazines.tagline: The world's oldest boxing weekly, and Britain's paper of record.

magazines.name: Boxing Magazine (Japan)
magazines.tagline: Japan's boxing monthly, covering title fights from Korakuen Hall to Bangkok.

magazines.name: World Boxing
magazines.tagline: From the Golden Gloves to the Olympics, the amateurs who will be the next champions.
